newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Thousands head to Kabul from Taleban town.
newsitem.headline: Thousands head to Kabul from Taleban town.

text.p: Thousands of Afghan civilians fled their homes north of Kabul on Tuesday, saying the Taleban militia who recently recaptured the town of Charikar had ordered them to leave, witnesses said.
Around 15,000 people fled to the Afghan capital over the weekend, U.N Deputy High Commissioner for Refugees Gerald Walzer told a meeting in the Turkmen capital Ashgabat.

The arrivals, mostly from Charikar, raise the total of displaced people from frontline areas north of Kabul since January 2 to more than 50,000, a statement by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said, quoting UNHCR monitoring posts on Kabul's outskirts.
"Through a loudspeaker, the Taleban ordered all the civilians to leave Charikar and we started packing and collecting what we could carry," said Shah Ghasi, a primary school teacher.
Observers believe the civilians have been ordered out for fear they will rebel and attack Taleban forces.
The road down to Kabul was dotted with women, children and the elderly. Some were ferried in trucks laden with people, some covering their faces with plastic sheeting against the extreme cold.
No immediate comment was available from leaders of the Taleban militia, who have said they were determined to disarm civilians in the town of Charikar and other recaptured villages.
A Taleban spokesman said earlier they had not ordered people in the newly captured area to leave.

The Taleban seized Charikar, about 50 km (30 miles) north of the capital, and the nearby Bagram military airbase last Thursday in a lightning offensive against forces loyal to General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Ahmad Shah Masood.
The Taleban captured the same territory soon after seizing Kabul in September but lost it after Masood, military commander in the ousted government, hit back with guerrilla tactics.
"We have known our enemy now and need to disarm them, and if not they will ambush us again," said a Taleban frontline commander early this week.
In their first drive north of Kabul in October the largely Pashtun Taleban faced resistance from locals north of Kabul who are mainly ethnic Tajiks.
Taleban commander Haji Feda Mohammad said his forces had to disarm the people because he said they abused the good intentions of the movement in not disarming them in October.
Women, clad in the all-embracing burqa made mandatory by the Taleban, carried small bundles of belongings on their heads.
Children bore infants and men drove heavily-laden donkeys as well as cattle along the icy road set against a forbidding backdrop of the snow-capped Hindu Kush mountains.
Life under the Taleban would be harsh, observers said, since they carried Dostum's banknotes, which are not valid in Kabul.
"I don't know what to do with these notes," said an old, exhausted-looking man with a child strapped to his back.
No accommodation for the displaced has been arranged by any aid agency.
"I believe that the situation of living for these people will be a nightmare," UNHCR official Terry Pitzner told reporters in Kabul.
There are tens of thousands of poverty-stricken people struggling to survive and there have been heavy snowfalls over the past few days.

According to new figures released by the UNHCR at the Ashgabat meeting, called to discuss the future of humanitarian aid for Afghanistan, at least 90,000 people have been displaced inside Afghanistan since the beginning of October, with a further 41,000 seeking refuge in Pakistan.
Walzer said this was probably a conservative figure as thousands of other people might have fled to areas where no monitoring took place.
Tens of thousands of people have also been displaced by Afghanistan's second battle front in the northwestern province of Badghis, where fighting also intensified last week.
